name: Christian humanism
summary: Christian humanism holds that human dignity, learning and freedom find their fullest foundation in Christian faith. Its Renaissance form (Erasmus, Colet) sought church and social reform through classical and biblical scholarship and peace among Christian princes; its twentieth-century political form (Maritain's integral humanism) defends natural rights, democracy and pluralism while rejecting both totalitarianism and secular humanism.
scope: Mainly the twentieth-century personalist strand, Jacques Maritain's 'integral Christian humanism' (with Mounier's circle), supplemented by the Erasmian northern Renaissance strand on peace, princes and reform. Excludes secular humanism, Italian Neoplatonic humanism's courtly strands, and confessional integralism. The ideology is partly a philosophy of the person, so economic and many modern-issue answers are low-confidence inferences.

keyFigures.name: Desiderius Erasmus
keyFigures.role: Leading northern Renaissance Christian humanist who pursued church reform through scholarship and argued for peace.

keyFigures.name: Jacques Maritain
keyFigures.role: Thomist philosopher who developed 'integral Christian humanism' and defended natural rights and democracy.

worker-ownership.rationale: Adherents are split: personalists have favoured worker participation and co-responsibility, but Maritain avoided committing to socialist ownership.

strong-leader.rationale: Maritain broke with Action Francaise over its anti-democratic nationalism and rejected fascism; the person may not be subordinated to a leader.

state-harmful.rationale: Maritain holds the state is a necessary instrument of the common good and treats authority as natural, so anarchism is foreign to it.

more-religion-public.rationale: Maritain envisioned a Christianly inspired polity in which religion and civic fraternities have a leading role, while pluralist and non-coercive.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Humanists valued cultural inheritance, yet Erasmus and Maritain looked past nation toward Christian and human unity; split.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Maritain supported a world federation of political societies and championed the Universal Declaration, provided states keep fair autonomy.

nation-first.rationale: Erasmus calls national hatreds artificial and urges Christians to unite as one; Maritain favoured wider federation.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Erasmus condemned nearly all war, while later Catholic just-war thinking allows defence of the innocent; adherents split.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Modern strands (including stewardship theology) lean in favour but classical sources are silent; split.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Maritain argued that a humanism lacking the spiritual dimension is merely partial, so technical progress alone cannot save humanity.

experts-over-public.rationale: Maritain held that authority derives from the people and their natural right to govern themselves.

central-planning.rationale: Maritain rejected communism and socialism and held the person cannot be subordinated to the state.

basic-income.rationale: No stated position; adherents split between solidarity with the poor and concern for work and responsibility.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Maritain rejected communism, whose aim this describes.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Maritain valued intermediate bodies and fraternities but opposed state domination, so state-recognised wage-setting finds mixed support.

one-party-rule.rationale: Maritain rejected fascism, communism and all totalitarian rule and affirmed democracy and pluralism.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Erasmus addressed princes and accepted monarchy as given, whereas Maritain defended democracy; split.

workers-councils.rationale: Maritain rejected communism and worked within a pluralist democratic order, not rule by councils.

natural-rulers.rationale: Maritain held that authority arises from the people and equal dignity of persons; rule is not a natural prerogative of some.

political-violence-never.rationale: Erasmus came near pacifism while the Thomist tradition accepts just war and resistance; adherents split.

war-builds-character.rationale: Erasmus calls war the worst of evils, contrary to nature and religion, and a calamity borne by the common people.

separate-church-state.rationale: Maritain proposed cooperation between church and state, each with its own sphere, rather than strict separation, while rejecting a confessional state.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Maritain grounds law in natural law known by reason and accessible to all, within a pluralist polity, not direct scriptural law.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The state is an instrument of the common good and justice is a public matter in this tradition.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Maritain opposed nationalism and affirmed the universal dignity of the person, and Erasmus held national hatreds artificial.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Maritain rejected Marxist communism and Christian humanism stresses cooperation and the common good.

civilizational-union.rationale: Erasmus urged Christian unity across kingdoms, whereas Maritain pointed to a wider world federation; split.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Personalism and Christian ethics treat the person as oriented to the common good and to love of others.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Maritain held that persons cannot be subordinated to society and that natural rights are inalienable and prior to the state, while also stressing duties.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Christian humanism prizes learning, culture and the classical heritage, which are incompatible with this.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Government is human self-rule and moral judgement in this tradition, so handing it to algorithms is alien.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Maritain grounded politics in natural law and principles rather than pragmatic outcomes alone.

direct-action.rationale: Maritain favoured democratic and civic means and Erasmus reformed through learning and persuasion.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: A Marxist aim that the tradition rejects.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Maritain rejected Marxism and its theory; Christian critique of abuses does not equate all profit with exploitation.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Maritain rejected communism and totalitarian dictatorship in favour of democratic personalism.

collective-farming.rationale: Collectivisation belongs to communism, which Maritain rejected.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Not a Christian humanist doctrine; Erasmus blamed princely ambition and hatreds, and Maritain rejected the Marxist analysis.

taxation-theft.rationale: Maritain holds the state serves the common good and authority is legitimate, so taxation is not theft.

harm-principle.rationale: Maritain held that law is tied to natural law and the common good, which can reach beyond preventing harm to others.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Rights belong to persons but the person is social and oriented to the common good, and Maritain recognised workers' and other associational rights.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Maritain held that the people's right to govern themselves is the heart of legitimate authority.

state-as-business.rationale: The state serves the common good, not customer satisfaction.

media-academia-power.rationale: Neither Erasmian nor Maritainian sources make any claim about media or university power, so adherents are genuinely split.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Maritain affirmed the equal dignity of all and denounced racism and antisemitism.

organic-representation.rationale: Maritain valued civic fraternities and intermediate bodies but within democratic representation; split.

total-state.rationale: Maritain rejected fascism and communism and held that the person cannot be subordinated to the state.

national-rebirth.rationale: Maritain broke with the nationalist Action Francaise and rejected fascism.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Erasmus condemned wars over dynastic claims and borders as the greatest evil.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Maritain grounded authority in the people, not in personal oaths of fealty.

bound-labor.rationale: Maritain's personalism holds that the person is never a mere instrument of another (s2), which excludes serfdom; no cited text discusses bound agricultural labour itself.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Christian humanists recovered classical learning in the confidence that truth can be recovered through philology and reason.

universal-morality.rationale: Maritain's natural law holds that universal first principles exist and can be recognised by all.

single-common-good.rationale: Maritain treats the common good as the basis of the state, yet he also defends a pluralist polity of differing convictions (s2), so how far adherents reject interest-balancing is contested.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal policy is outside what Erasmus or Maritain addressed, and adherents hold varied economic views.

rule-by-example.rationale: Erasmus stressed the prince's example and wisdom but also law and arbitration, and Maritain relied on democratic institutions; split.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Christian humanism holds faith and reason as complementary and rejects the exclusive reliance on reason that defines secular humanism.

class-collaboration.rationale: Personalism is a via media between individualism and socialism and rejects class struggle in favour of the common good.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Christian humanism is defined by recovering classical and patristic heritage and learning.

workers-nation.rationale: The national-versus-international organisation of labour is a socialist debate this tradition did not engage.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Maritain rejected Marxism and holds the state serves the common good.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiratorial claim at odds with Maritain's opposition to antisemitism and his humane stance.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Erasmus and Colet did criticise corrupt clerics and princes, but a general populist charge is not a core claim.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Maritain assigned the state a positive role in the common good and workers' rights.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Equal dignity of persons and inalienable natural rights are central to Maritain's personalism and to the Universal Declaration he championed.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist debate foreign to the tradition; Maritain rejected socialism.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Maritain stressed freedom of conscience and a pluralist polity.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Maritain argued that authority derives from the people, who have a natural right to govern themselves.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Erasmus came near to this, but the Thomist tradition allows just coercion by the state; split.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Erasmus holds that humans were made for mutual aid and condemns strife.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Maritain defended pluralism, yet opposed totalitarian movements; split.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Maritain's pluralism holds that people of differing convictions can cooperate on shared practical aims.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Not endorsed; Maritain favoured elected representation.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Rights are inalienable and prior to the state in Maritain's natural-rights thought.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Naturalisation periods are a technical question outside the sources, so adherents are split.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Christian humanists differed by confession (Catholic and Protestant); split.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: A Leninist doctrine alien to the tradition.

recall-officials.rationale: Maritain's sources discuss democratic authority but not recall mechanisms, so the answer is genuinely open.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Natural law is universal, but Maritain's pluralism respects cultural difference; split.

death-penalty.rationale: Catholic-influenced adherents split; the tradition has historically allowed but modern strands oppose.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Maritain stressed freedom of conscience and accommodation of differing religious conscience.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Maritain rejected authoritarian rule and holds rights inalienable.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Maritain held natural rights are oriented toward the common good, and Christian social thought treats property as having a social function.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Erasmus condemned conquest and border redrawing without regard for the people governed.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Maritain proposed cooperating church and state, each in its own sphere, and rejected totalitarian control.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Maritain held authority derives from the people; Erasmus addressed princes as fallible and obliged to serve the people.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist thesis foreign to the tradition.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Contradicts Maritain's anti-nationalism and Erasmus's condemnation of conquest.

women-must-cover.rationale: State compulsion of this kind contradicts freedom of conscience.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Ethnolinguistic unification is a nationalist aim not found in Christian humanist sources.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: A Marxist thesis that Maritain's spiritual integral humanism rejects.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Maritain held natural rights are inalienable and prior to society, so majorities cannot override them.

patriotic-education.rationale: Erasmus distrusted national hatreds, whereas modest loyalty could be accepted; split.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Whether capitalism can avoid collapse is a Marxist-framed question the sources do not engage.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist thesis foreign to the tradition.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Maritain held rights are inalienable and championed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

elective-rulers.rationale: Maritain held authority derives from the people.

minority-veto.rationale: Maritain valued the role of dissenting minorities but accepted majority democracy.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Maritain held that positive law contradicting natural law is not true law, which supports resistance to lawless rule.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Erasmus urged princes to govern for the people and Christian duty binds the privileged to the needy.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Maritain developed a politically engaged integral humanism and Erasmus urged learned engagement in reform.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Gramscian hegemony theory is not engaged by the tradition, so no answer follows from the sources.

party-own-road.rationale: A communist-movement question that Christian humanism, which rejects communism, does not engage.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Maritain rejected fascism and its nationalism and supported democracy.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Maritain rejected both fascism and communism as inhuman.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Maritain held rights and democracy universal but accommodated pluralism; split.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Not endorsed; Maritain's democracy is representative, expressing the people's will through leaders.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Maritain held that a humanism lacking the spiritual dimension is partial, and Christian ethics criticises acquisitiveness.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Erasmus condemned wars of domination and Maritain backed international law.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Erasmus holds princes must govern for the people and Maritain holds that positive law contradicting natural law is not true law.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Maritain grounded law in natural law, so unjust laws lose moral force, but he still held that just law binds the conscience and rejected a general disclaimer.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Maritain opposed antisemitism and defended pluralism, so he rejected conspiracy theories against minorities.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Christian humanism treats marriage as a sacrament and a social foundation of the person, so it opposes abolishing it as a legal institution.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Maritain defended a world federation and universal rights above the state, and Erasmus decried narrow national interests, so national law over international is rejected.

religious-nation.rationale: Maritain's pluralism rejects a state defined by one religion, and he favoured a democratic order in which people of different beliefs cooperate.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Maritain defended private property as a natural right yet limited it by the common good; the sources opened do not settle where he draws the line for productive property.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Maritain's pluralism and subsidiarity favour a range of independent bodies serving the common good within a framework of public concern.

religion-illusion.rationale: Christian humanism holds that human dignity is founded in faith, so it rejects the view that religion is only consolation that fades.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Maritain's pluralism favours many associations within a state, not reorganising society into communal-property communities.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Maritain's integral humanism rejects both liberal individualism and totalitarian collectivism and seeks a different, personalist order.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Maritain defends democracy, natural rights and pluralism and rejects totalitarianism, which rules out suppressing opposition.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Nothing in the sources addresses sovereign debt or the IMF, and Christian humanists are split on it.

property-franchise.rationale: Maritain grounds democracy in the equal dignity and natural rights of every person, which rules out wealth qualifications for voting.

domination-women-nature.rationale: The personalist tradition does not treat the two forms of domination as one; adherents differ and the sources are silent.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Maritain's natural-law politics holds that rulers are bound by law grounded in justice, and that arbitrary decrees are not true law.

racial-franchise.rationale: Maritain's natural rights belong to every person as a person, so an ethnic franchise contradicts the core doctrine.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Maritain's equal dignity of persons and cooperation across religious convictions rule out singling out a minority for shunning.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Maritain rejects totalitarianism and secular humanism and defends religious freedom and pluralism.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Christian humanists are split by denomination, and the Catholic Maritain tradition and Protestant strands differ.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Maritain accepts just war and self-defence while Erasmus condemns war, so adherents mostly reject an absolute ban.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Maritain distinguishes the spiritual from the temporal and aims at a pluralist civic order, not politics as holy war.

god-not-male.rationale: Tradition mostly keeps male language for God but also holds God beyond sex; adherents are split.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Maritain's rights-based pluralism rests on the equal dignity of every person, rejecting economic dominance by a majority.

local-essentials-public.rationale: No documented position; adherents vary between pluralist public and private provision.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Maritain favoured world federation and pluralism, but nothing is documented on non-governing confederal councils.

person-over-state.rationale: Maritain's personalism holds that the person is never merely a means to the community or state.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Integral humanism rests on human dignity grounded in faith and a spiritual end beyond politics.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Maritain defended universal rights and opposed antisemitism, rejecting politics organised by race.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Erasmus's Complaint of Peace condemns war among Christian princes.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Personalism stresses the equal dignity of persons and does not single out women's distinct values; adherents are not clearly one way.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Maritain defended workers' rights and free association as part of the dignity of the person and the common good.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Maritain rejected totalitarianism and revolution and defended a pluralist democratic state.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Maritain favoured pluralism but also a defined personalist, communitarian economy; adherents are split.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Maritain grounded human dignity and natural rights in a common human nature given by God; this is central to his humanism.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Maritain held that the Christian faith is the fullest truth and defended pluralism without relativism, so the claim that all religions express one truth is rejected.

voter-id.rationale: Maritain defended democracy and the rights of the person but nothing in the sources addresses ballot identification; adherents could go either way.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Maritain grounds democracy in natural rights and the dignity of the person, so it requires moral substance beyond fair elections.

national-church-status.rationale: Maritain's pluralist democracy and defence of religious freedom point against a privileged legal position for one church.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Maritain grounds natural rights and the dignity of every person in Christian faith, so killing without trial is rejected.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Maritain defends pluralist democracy and intermediate bodies and rejects totalitarian leader rule, so bypassing parties and groups is rejected.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Maritain's natural-law personalism holds that law gets its authority from justice, in the tradition that an unjust law is no true law.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Maritain defends democracy and pluralism and rejects totalitarianism, so a communist-party-led system is opposed.

missingStatements.text: Peace among nations should be pursued by arbitration rather than war, and wars of princely ambition are never justified.
missingStatements.rationale: Erasmus urges settling disputes by arbitration and condemns dynastic wars as the worst of evils.
missingStatements.declined: Arbitration over war is a narrow peace-politics view; empower-international-orgs and political-violence-never do not match it closely enough.

missingStatements.text: Human rights are grounded in a natural law that exists independently of any government's decrees.
missingStatements.rationale: Maritain bases inalienable natural rights on natural law and holds that contrary positive law is not true law.

missingStatements.text: People who disagree about religion and ultimate beliefs can cooperate on shared practical aims in a pluralist society.
missingStatements.rationale: Maritain developed a theory of cooperation across differing convictions in a pluralist polity.
missingStatements.declined: Pluralist cooperation is near-universally endorsed, so it would not be contested; separate-church-state and equal-moral-worth cover its substance.

notes: Renaissance and modern strands differ: Erasmus addressed princes within monarchy, while Maritain defended democracy. Confessional differences (Catholic and Protestant) split moral issues; most answers on economy and modern controversies are inferences. Sources opened did not address economics or property in detail.
